xrefcode.com / docs / cli / field

$ xref field

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com
On this page
  1. Usage
  2. Arguments and options
  3. Examples
  4. One key: which layouts emit it
  5. An exact set of keys
  6. A subset of keys
  7. Machine-readable output

  9. Performance and caching
  10. Limits
  11. Provenance

Recover the in-memory layout behind serialized keys. Give field the keys a program prints (JSON object keys, for example) and it finds the serializer code that emits them, the offset of each field relative to the serialized value, and, with --write, candidate code that writes those fields.

Use it on a stripped binary when you know what a structure looks like on the wire and need to know where its fields live in memory: to read them with xref live memscan, watch writes to them, or find the code that updates them.

Usage

xref field [OPTIONS] [NAME]

Query one key (NAME) to see every layout that emits it, or an exact set of sibling keys with --keys a,b,c.

Arguments and options

Arguments

[NAME]
Single serialized key to query.

Options

--keys <KEYS>
Exact comma-separated set of sibling serialized keys (--keys c,m,e).
--within <WITHIN>
Only functions containing this address or symbol.
--json
Emit the structured report as JSON.
--min-offsets <MIN_OFFSETS>
Require this many distinct serialized offsets on the same input root in an accessor.
default 2
--min-keys <MIN_KEYS>
Accept a key-set candidate matching at least N requested keys; defaults to the full set.
--exhaustive-key-seeds
Include partial key-reference seeds even when no direct-call path combines them.
--max-functions <MAX_FUNCTIONS>
Maximum sibling helper functions selected into the discovery context (1..=8192).
default 4096
--max-instructions <MAX_INSTRUCTIONS>
Maximum decoded instructions per function for key/value analysis (1..=16384).
default 4096
--write
Show accessor instructions that may write the queried field.
--writes-all-of <WRITES_ALL_OF>
Require writes to every comma-separated field name.
--writer-root <WRITER_ROOT>
Only writers whose offsets are relative to this kind of pointer (returned: a pointer returned by a call, such as a map lookup). Values: any (Any root); argument (An ABI argument register on entry (rdi, rsi, …)); returned (A pointer returned by a call (call lookup; mov r, rax; mov [r+off], …)); loaded (A pointer loaded from memory (mov r, [p+off]; mov [r+off], …)).
default any
--limit <LIMIT>
Maximum accessor rows (1..=128).
default 64
--layout-only
Skip the global accessor search while inspecting layout evidence.

Examples

The examples use the official ripgrep 14.1.1 release binary. With --json, ripgrep ends a search with statistics such as:

JSON
{"elapsed":{"secs":0,"nanos":143000,"human":"0.000143s"},"searches":2,"searches_with_match":1,
 "bytes_searched":4104,"bytes_printed":293,"matched_lines":3,"matches":3}

One key: which layouts emit it

Command
$ xref -b rg field searches --within 0x1835f0 --layout-only
Output

      key_value_call 0x1835f0 0x183700 -> call 0x158e60
  caveat: input_argument_relationship_not_concrete_rust_type
  caveat: minimum_extent_is_addressed_span_not_allocation_or_exact_type_size

limitation: exact size, alignment, tail padding, skipped fields and allocator identity are unknown
limitation: only supported x86-64 SysV integer arguments and known static helper entry targets are summarized

stderr
xref: load 4.1ms, total 10.3ms

--within 0x1835f0 limits the search to one function (found with refs); without it field searches reports every function that emits the key (16 on this binary). --layout-only skips the writer search.

How to read it:

  • layout 0: 0x1835f0..0x18374c base=rdi — the serializer function and the argument register its offsets are relative to: on entry rdi points to the serialized value.
  • "searches" -> 0x0, "searches_with_match" -> 0x8, … "elapsed" -> 0x30 — each emitted key and the offset of its value from base. instruction-read-widths=[8] is how many bytes the code reads there.
  • key 0x492c12 len=8 via rsi value=rcx — the evidence: the key string address and length are passed in rsi/rdx and the field address in rcx to call 0x158e60 at 0x183664 (key_value_call).
  • order: lexical_call_site_order… — keys are listed in call order, which is not necessarily the declaration order.
  • caveat:, limitation: and coverage: lines state what the result does not prove and how much of the binary was analysed.

So ripgrep's statistics structure keeps searches at +0x0, searches_with_match at +0x8, bytes_searched at +0x10, bytes_printed at +0x18, matched_lines at +0x20, matches at +0x28 and elapsed at +0x30, which matches the pseudo-C of the same function on the c page.

xref: load 3.4ms, total 63.4ms

--keys asks for layouts that emit exactly these sibling keys. The key diagnostics lines show, per key, the functions that reference the string (refs) and those that emit it (emissions). The full output (cut above) lists eight layouts: the four direct serializers at 0x1835f0, 0x183750, 0x183dd0, 0x183f20 (base=rdi) and four callers that reach them through a helper (base=rcx).

elapsed is itself a structure (secs, nanos), so its own keys appear in the layouts too ("nanos" -> 0x38). Keys inside a requested value do not count against the exact set; in xref 0.4.0 they still did, and this query returned no layout.

A subset of keys

--keys is exact: a layout with more top-level keys than requested is not a match.

Command
$ xref -b rg field --keys searches,bytes_searched --layout-only
Output
"searches,bytes_searched": 0 layout candidates, 0 accessor candidates; not_found_under_limits

xref: load 3.3ms, total 29.2ms

No layout emits only these two keys, so the result is empty. The status says not_found_under_limits because some functions could not be fully analysed (warning: unsupported_cfg_or_instruction_budget_scopes_omitted), not because the budget was too small; raising --max-instructions would not help here. To search by a subset, lower --min-keys:

Command
$ xref -b rg field --keys searches,bytes_searched --min-keys 1 --layout-only
Output
"searches,bytes_searched": 16 layout candidates, 0 accessor candidates; candidates
key diagnostics: min-matches=1 max-functions=4096 max-instructions=4096 incomplete=true budget-exhausted=false

matched keys and missing keys show how each layout relates to the request. With --min-keys 1 every layout that emits either key is listed, so expect many candidates.

The JSON report (schema_version: 1) carries the same evidence: candidates[].fields[] with offset, instruction_read_widths and emissions[].evidence_steps[] (function, instruction, assembly, role), plus coverage, limitations and, with --write, accessor_candidates. The MCP server returns the same report for {"operation": "field", ...}.

With --write, field searches the whole binary for functions that write the same offsets relative to one pointer, ranks them and prints up to --limit (accessor: blocks, after the layouts). --writes-all-of keeps writers that store every named field. Each accessor line shows the function, the base register and the matching offsets, then three lines:

  • rank: score=… colocated-writes=… callgraph-distance=…;
  • score: with every term of the score, which add up to it;
  • lead: with the gap to the next listed function and the terms it comes from.

A lead made of one term, such as callgraph alone, is thin: the runner-up is equal on everything else. The terms are described in Serialized field search. The lines after these are the store instructions.

The same function is listed once per layout it matches (layout=0, layout=1, …), so with eight layouts the three rows here are one function. Read the result critically. Here the top candidate, 0x3a6e50, writes offsets 0x0…0x38 of some 64-byte structure, including immediate values (mov dword ptr [rbx+0x18], 0xa) that do not look like statistics counters: an offset pattern shared by many structures is not proof of the same type (same_root_offset_constellation_not_type_proof). Its lead line says how thin the rank is: +2 over 0x2464e0..0x2466b5 (callgraph +2). The next function scores the same on every instruction term and is one call edge farther from the serializer. Check a candidate with c before relying on it, look at the runner-up, or restrict the pointer kind with --writer-root returned|argument|loaded.

Performance and caching

A whole-image search builds an index of references, direct calls and writer facts under $XDG_CACHE_HOME/xref/field-index-v1 and reuses it for other keys. An identical command on an unchanged binary replays the stored report; on Unix a background field-daemon answers later queries for the same binary. Details: Field key search.

Limits

  • Offsets are relative to the serialized value as passed to the serializer, not necessarily to the start of a heap allocation.
  • Only the x86-64 SysV integer-argument call model and known helper entry points are followed; opaque calls and unusual code generation may hide a layout. An empty result is not proof that the structure does not exist.
  • Writer ranking is a heuristic over offset patterns, not type proof.

Provenance

Recorded with a development build of xref after 0.4.0 on Linux x86-64, on rg = ripgrep 14.1.1 (official stripped release). Output is unchanged except that whitespace at the end of each line and empty lines at the end of the output are removed; long outputs are cut where marked.
